title: The Nonverbal Glass Ceiling
hook: The same raised voice or flash of anger can win one person respect and cost another theirs, and a fair reader learns to see the difference.
why:
Most of this book is about reading other people more accurately. This chapter is about a particular way in which reading goes wrong at work: the same behaviour, from different people, is read differently. A man who raises his voice in a meeting may be seen as passionate and committed, while a woman who does the same may be seen as emotional or difficult. A tall man may be judged a natural leader before he has said a word. An idea may be ignored when one person offers it and praised when another repeats it.

These are not only questions of fairness, though they are that. They are also questions of accuracy. If you read a colleague's anger as a flaw in her character when it is a response to a real problem, you have misread her, and you may miss the problem too. This chapter looks at the research on anger and status, on influence in groups, on when assertive women are penalised and when they are not, on height and other accidents of the body, on interruptions, and on credit for ideas. It ends with what a fair reader, and especially a man in a position to notice, can actually do.

teach.p:
In 2008 Victoria Brescoll and Eric Uhlmann showed people videos of a job candidate describing a time when a colleague's mistake had lost them an important account. In some versions the candidate described it with anger, in others with sadness or without emotion. The words were the same. Only the candidate's gender and emotion changed.

Men who expressed anger were given more status than men who expressed sadness, and were judged to deserve a higher salary and more authority. Women who expressed anger were given less status than women who did not, and less than angry men. This held even when the woman was described as a senior executive rather than a trainee. The chapter on the ethics of reading people in Part VI mentioned this study in passing. Its most important finding is the reason behind the gap.

People explained the two angers differently. A man's anger was put down to the situation: something had gone wrong and he was responding to it. A woman's anger was put down to her character: she was an angry or out-of-control person. When the researchers gave an outside reason for the woman's anger, such as a colleague having lied, the gap in status disappeared.

This is a reading error, and it is one you can catch in yourself. When someone at work expresses anger, the first useful question is not what kind of person they are but what has happened. The figure here makes a firm, chopping gesture, the kind that accompanies a strong point. Whether it reads as conviction or as loss of control often depends on who is making it, and that is the reader's problem, not the speaker's.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if angry men and angry women were given the same status when describing the same events. In Brescoll and Uhlmann's study they were not, until the woman's anger was given an outside cause.
teach.pullQuote: When someone at work is angry, ask what has happened before you ask what kind of person they are.

teach.p:
Status is one thing; influence is another. In 2015 Jessica Salerno and Liana Peter-Hagene asked whether anger changes how persuasive a person is in a group. Participants took part in what they believed was an online mock jury deliberating on a murder case. In fact the other jurors' messages were scripted. In each group, one juror held out against the majority, and in some versions the holdout expressed anger.

When the holdout was a man and expressed anger, participants became less confident in their own verdict: the angry man was pulling them towards his view. When the holdout was a woman and expressed exactly the same anger, in the same words, participants became more confident in their own verdict. Her anger made her less persuasive. The researchers found that people drew different conclusions from the two angers, which fits Brescoll and Uhlmann's finding about where people locate the cause.

The study is striking because nothing about the holdouts differed except a name. The participants never saw or heard them. The gap lay entirely in how the same emotion was interpreted.

For anyone who runs meetings or makes decisions with others, this suggests a simple check. When someone argues a minority view with feeling, ask whether you are weighing the argument or reacting to the feeling, and whether you would react the same way if someone else had said it. The figure here makes a firm, palm-down gesture, as if pressing a point. The gesture is the same whoever makes it. The reading need not be.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if angry men and angry women holding the same minority view were equally persuasive. In Salerno and Peter-Hagene's study, anger increased men's influence and reduced women's, though the deliberation was online and scripted.

teach.p:
It is often said that women who behave assertively at work face a backlash: they are seen as competent but cold, and disliked for it. In 2016 Melissa Williams and Larissa Tiedens combined the results of dozens of studies to see how strong this backlash is and when it happens.

They found that dominant behaviour did make women less liked than men behaving the same way, though the overall effect was small. It also reduced their chances of being hired, by a larger margin. It did not change how competent they were judged to be. The penalty was about liking, not ability.

The most interesting finding was about the kind of dominance. When dominance was explicit, such as direct demands, open disagreement or telling others what to do, women were penalised. When it was implicit, expressed through the body rather than words, such as steady eye contact, an upright posture or a firm voice, there was no penalty at all. The researchers suggested that people punish behaviour they clearly see as breaking a stereotype, and nonverbal dominance is less likely to be seen that way.

It would be easy to turn this into advice for women: be assertive with your body, not your words. That puts the burden in the wrong place. The more useful lesson for the reader is that the penalty is in the evaluator. Explicit, direct assertiveness is a normal part of working life, and if you find yourself liking a woman less for doing what you would admire in a man, the problem is in your reading. The figure here meets the viewer's eyes directly, the kind of implicit dominance that, in these studies, carried no penalty for anyone.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if women were penalised as heavily for nonverbal dominance as for explicit dominance. Williams and Tiedens found a penalty for explicit dominance but none for implicit, nonverbal dominance.

teach.p:
Some of the signals people read as authority are not behaviour at all. They are accidents of the body. In 2004 Timothy Judge and Daniel Cable analysed four large studies of height and work. Taller people earned more, even after accounting for gender, weight and age: each extra inch was worth, on average, several hundred dollars a year. The link was strongest in sales and management, jobs where being seen as a leader matters most.

The chapter on the spine as status in Part I made the point that a tall man has claimed nothing by being tall. The pay data shows that others nonetheless treat height as a sign of something, and this bias falls on short men as much as on women. A short man who speaks with authority may be read as overcompensating, while a tall man saying the same thing is read as a natural leader.

Faces matter too. In 2009 Robert Livingston and Nicholas Pearce found that Black chief executives tended to have more babyish faces than white chief executives, and suggested that a face read as warm and unthreatening may help Black men overcome stereotypes in reaching senior roles. The finding is one study and is debated, and a chapter in Part V on how Black men's bodies are read takes up these questions properly. But it shows how a feature nobody chose can shape how a person's authority is received.

The practical lesson is to notice when your sense of who seems like a leader is responding to height, face or voice rather than to what people do. The figure here stands upright, seen in profile. How tall he looks tells you nothing about how well he leads.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if height were unrelated to pay and perceived leadership once other factors were accounted for. Judge and Cable found a consistent link across four large samples.

teach.p:
Interruption is partly a nonverbal act. Before anyone speaks over another person, there is usually a lean forward, an intake of breath, a hand lifting, a mouth opening. Whoever acts on those signals most readily tends to hold the floor.

In 2017 Tonja Jacobi and Dylan Schweers studied fifteen years of transcripts from oral arguments at the United States Supreme Court, where justices question lawyers and each other. Female justices were interrupted around three times as often as male justices, by both male justices and male lawyers, even though the female justices spoke less overall. The gap grew rather than shrank as more women joined the court. The study used transcripts, so it captured words rather than tone, but the pattern was large and consistent.

Research on everyday conversation gives a more mixed picture, with differences that are often small and depend on the setting, the topic and the people involved. Interruptions are not always hostile; some are enthusiastic agreement. But in settings where status is at stake, being cut off repeatedly is costly, and it is not evenly shared.

There is a simple discipline here for anyone, and especially for men, who are on average more likely to make the intrusive kind of interruption. When you feel the lean forward and the breath before speaking, check whether the other person has finished. If you interrupt, notice and hand the floor back: Sorry, go on. If you are chairing and someone is cut off, return to them by name. The figure here raises a hand, the orderly way of asking for a turn rather than taking one.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if female justices were interrupted no more often than male justices. Jacobi and Schweers found they were interrupted around three times as often, though everyday conversation shows smaller and more variable differences.

teach.p:
A familiar meeting story goes like this. A woman makes a suggestion and it passes without comment. Ten minutes later a man makes the same suggestion and it is praised. Nobody intended it. The idea simply landed differently the second time, perhaps because of who said it, how loudly, or from which seat.

In 2016 the Washington Post reported how women working in the Obama White House responded to this. When one of them made a key point, another would repeat it, crediting her by name. They called it amplification. It made it harder for the point to be overlooked, and harder for anyone else to claim it. According to the report, the President noticed and began calling on women and junior staff more often.

This is a practice, not a study, but it rests on the principles in this chapter and the last. Ideas need to be seen and heard to count, and the body and voice that carry an idea affect whether it lands. Repeating someone's point and naming them borrows your own visibility for their idea.

Anyone can do this, and it costs nothing. When a colleague's point is ignored, return to it: I want to come back to what Sara said. When someone repeats an idea that was already offered, credit it: That's close to Sara's point earlier. Listening fully, with your body turned towards the speaker, is part of it too. The figure here listens with attention, the posture that tells a speaker her words are landing.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if ideas were credited in meetings equally, whoever first offered them. The fact that the White House staff felt they needed amplification suggests they were not, though the evidence here is a report of practice rather than a study.

teach.p:
None of the biases in this chapter is something a person chooses. They work in the speed of a first impression, below deliberate thought, which is exactly why they need deliberate checks. Several are simple enough to use in the moment.

The first is the swap test. When you find yourself reading someone's behaviour as too emotional, too aggressive, too soft or too pushy, imagine the same words and gestures from someone of a different gender, height or background, and ask whether you would read them the same way. If not, look again at what actually happened.

The second is to look for the situation. Anger, tears, raised voices and silence all have causes. Asking what happened before deciding what kind of person someone is corrects the very attribution error Brescoll and Uhlmann found.

The third is to watch the floor. Notice who speaks, who is interrupted, whose ideas are picked up and who looks at whom when a question is asked. In a mixed group, people often address their answers to the most senior or most confident-seeming person in the room, and that is frequently a man. Turning your body and gaze to whoever asked the question is a small correction.

The fourth is to use whatever advantage you have. If you are tall, senior, male or confident in a room, people's eyes tend to rest on you. You can use that to give others the floor. The figure here sits turned towards a colleague, giving her his full attention. Small acts of attention like this are where fair reading becomes fair practice.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if deliberate checks like the swap test made no difference to how behaviour is read. They do not remove bias, but they give a slower, more accurate reading a chance to correct a fast one.

poseGallery.doCaption: Handing the floor back with an open hand
poseGallery.dontCaption: Taking the floor by pointing over someone
poseGallery.annotation: When you notice you have cut someone off, hand the floor back. Sorry, go on, with an open hand, costs nothing.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Leaning back while a colleague presents
poseGallery.annotation: Ideas land partly through the listeners. A body that is visibly attending tells the speaker, and the room, that her point counts.

poseGallery.doCaption: Turned towards the speaker until she is done
poseGallery.dontCaption: Looking away before she has finished
poseGallery.annotation: Looking away early signals that a turn is over. Staying turned towards the speaker holds the floor open for her.

poseGallery.doCaption: Turning to the person who asked
poseGallery.dontCaption: Answering the man when the woman asked
poseGallery.annotation: Where you look when you answer tells the room who counts. Face the person who asked the question.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sitting back until she has finished
poseGallery.dontCaption: Leaning in to take the floor mid-sentence
poseGallery.annotation: Interruption starts in the body: a lean, a breath, a lifted hand. Notice the lean and let the sentence end.

caseStudy:
Tom, thirty-eight, leads a project team of seven. In his written feedback for the year, he described Claire, one of his senior engineers, as sharp but too emotional in meetings. He described Mark, another senior engineer, as passionate and a strong voice. When his own manager read both reviews, she asked him what each had actually done.

Tom thought about it. In the meeting he remembered most clearly, Mark had slammed a hand on the table over a supplier's missed deadline. Claire, a week later, had said sharply that the team was being asked to ship code that had not been tested. He realised he had read Mark's anger as commitment and Claire's as a flaw, and that Claire had been right: the untested code had caused an outage a month later.

He tried the swap test on his other reviews and found two more places where he had used different words for similar behaviour. He rewrote them. He also started watching his own meetings more closely. Over two weeks he counted how often each person was cut off. Claire was interrupted more than anyone, often by Mark and sometimes by Tom himself.

He did not announce a policy. He simply began returning to people who had been cut off, by name, and crediting ideas to whoever first offered them. When he caught himself leaning in to speak over someone, he sat back and waited. Claire noticed within a month and said so, a little warily. Mark did not notice at all, but he was interrupted a little more often himself, and found he did not much like it.
observe: Notice the words you use to describe colleagues' emotions, and whether you use different words for similar behaviour from different people.
Notice who is interrupted in your next meeting, by whom, and whether anyone returns to them.
Notice when an idea is offered twice in a meeting, and who receives the credit.
Notice where your eyes go when someone asks a question in a group, and whether you look at the person who asked.

drills.name: Swap Test
steps: Think of three colleagues whose behaviour you have recently judged as too emotional, too aggressive or too soft.
For each, write down exactly what they said and did.
Imagine the same words and gestures from someone of a different gender, height or seniority.
Where it does, write a fairer description of what happened.
variations: Run the swap test on a colleague you admire as well as one you find difficult, since the bias can flatter as well as penalise.
Swap age or seniority instead of gender for one reading this week, and see whether your description of the behaviour changes.
Ask a trusted colleague to run the swap test on one of your written reviews, and listen to what they find.

drills.name: Interruption Count
steps: In your next two meetings, keep a quiet tally of interruptions: who cut off whom.
Afterwards, look for patterns by gender, seniority and seat.
Choose one person you will make a point of returning to next time.
Note whether you interrupt less once you are counting.
variations: Count interruptions in a hybrid meeting and note whether the people on the screen are cut off more than those in the room.
Count only your own interruptions for a week, and note the moments just before you cut in.
Share your counts, without names, with the person who chairs the meeting, and suggest one change.

drills.name: Amplify Once
steps: In your next meeting, listen for a good point that passes without comment.
Later in the meeting, come back to it and name the person who made it.
If someone repeats an earlier idea, credit the person who first offered it.
Afterwards, note how the room responded.
variations: Agree with one colleague that you will each amplify the other at least once in your next shared meeting, then compare notes.
Amplify a point from someone more junior than you, and notice whether the room's response to it changes.
Notice whether anyone amplifies your points, and thank them afterwards, so that the practice spreads.

drills.name: Situation First
steps: The next time a colleague expresses anger or frustration at work, pause before forming a view of them.
Ask yourself, or them, what has happened.
Write down the situation as they see it.
Decide whether the anger was a reasonable response to that situation.
Compare this with your first impression.
variations: Apply the same steps to a colleague's tears or silence, not only to anger, and see whether your first reading changes.
Write down the situation behind your own most recent display of frustration at work, and ask whether others would have known it.
Ask the person directly, when appropriate, "What happened before that meeting?", and listen before you decide what it meant.

quiz.q: A colleague says that people judge anger at work the same way whoever expresses it. What did Brescoll and Uhlmann find?
options: Angry women were given more status than angry men, because their anger seemed more unusual
Angry men gained status and angry women lost it, unless the woman's anger had an outside cause
Anger cost everyone status equally, whatever their gender or seniority in the organisation
Anger had no effect on status, because people paid attention only to the words being used
quiz.explain: Men's anger was put down to the situation and women's to their character. When the researchers gave an outside reason for the woman's anger, the gap disappeared.

quiz.q: In Salerno and Peter-Hagene's mock jury study, what happened when a holdout juror expressed anger?
options: Anger made both male and female holdouts more persuasive to others
Anger made both male and female holdouts less persuasive to others
Anger made men more persuasive and women less, though their words were identical
Anger had no effect, because the other jurors could not see the holdout's face at all
quiz.explain: Participants became less sure of their own verdict when a man expressed anger, and more sure when a woman expressed the same anger in the same words. People drew different conclusions about the cause of the same emotion.

quiz.q: According to Williams and Tiedens's review, when were women penalised for dominant behaviour?
options: Mostly for nonverbal dominance such as eye contact, and seldom for anything they said
For both kinds equally, and also in how competent they were judged to be
Never, because the penalty disappeared once all the studies were combined
For explicit dominance such as direct demands, but not for nonverbal dominance
quiz.explain: Explicit dominance reduced how much women were liked and their chances of being hired, though not how competent they seemed. Implicit, nonverbal dominance such as eye contact carried no penalty.

quiz.q: What did Judge and Cable find about height and work?
options: Taller people earned more, even with gender, weight and age accounted for
Height mattered only for men, and only in jobs that required physical strength
Shorter people earned more, because they were seen as harder working than others
Height had no link with pay once education had been fully taken into account
quiz.explain: Across four large samples, each extra inch was linked to higher pay, with the strongest link in sales and management. The bias affects short men as well as women.

quiz.q: A colleague makes a good suggestion that passes without comment. Ten minutes later a senior man says the same thing and is praised. What fits this chapter best?
options: Say nothing, because pointing it out would only embarrass the senior man
Credit the idea to her, and ask her to say more about it in the meeting
Praise the senior man as well, so that the meeting keeps its momentum
Raise it with her privately afterwards, and suggest she speak more loudly
quiz.explain: Returning to the original speaker and naming her is amplification. It makes the idea harder to overlook and the credit harder to lose, without making a scene.

quiz.q: Writing reviews, you notice that you called a female colleague too emotional and a male colleague passionate. What is the best first step?
options: Write down what each did, and ask whether you would use the same word if they swapped
Delete both words, because emotions should never be mentioned in any written review
Keep the words, since first impressions are usually the most accurate ones we form
Ask other colleagues which word they would use, and then go along with the majority
quiz.explain: The swap test separates what someone did from how you read it. If the same behaviour would earn different words from a different person, the description needs to change.

quiz.q: In Brescoll and Uhlmann's study, what closed the gap in status between angry men and angry women?
options: Telling participants that the woman was more senior than the man in the video
Giving an outside reason for the woman's anger, such as a colleague having lied
Having the woman express her anger more quietly and with fewer words than the man
Showing the videos to participants who worked in the same industry as the candidates
quiz.explain: People put women's anger down to character and men's to circumstance. When the researchers gave a situational reason for the woman's anger, the gap in status disappeared.

quiz.q: In a meeting, a supplier answers a woman's technical question by looking at and addressing her junior male colleague. What fits this chapter best?
options: The junior should say nothing, since correcting a supplier would be embarrassing for him
The junior can turn towards her, name her role and look at her, handing the answer back
The woman should ask her junior colleague to put all her questions to the supplier for her
Nobody should react, since where people look when they answer has no effect on the meeting
quiz.explain: People often answer whoever seems most senior, frequently a man. Turning your body and gaze to the person who asked, and naming her role, uses your visibility to return the floor to her.

quiz.q: Someone says that interruptions of female justices at the United States Supreme Court faded as more women joined the court. What did Jacobi and Schweers find?
options: That the gap grew rather than shrank as more women joined the court
That the gap disappeared entirely once there were three female justices
That male justices were interrupted more often than female justices by lawyers
That the study could not measure interruptions because it used written transcripts
quiz.explain: Female justices were interrupted around three times as often as male justices, and the gap grew rather than shrank as more women joined the court. The study used transcripts, so it captured words rather than tone.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific colleague whose emotion, assertiveness or manner at work you have judged in the past year. Write down exactly what they said and did, as a camera would have recorded it. Now imagine the same words and gestures from someone of a different gender, height or seniority. Would you have described them the same way? Then describe one meeting in which you could notice who is interrupted or whose ideas are credited, and what you will do there.
reflection.guidance: Everyone carries these biases; finding one in yourself is a sign the check is working, not a sign of bad character. Be specific about the behaviour itself, separate from your judgment of it. If the swap test changes your reading, write the fairer description down, because that is the one worth acting on.

failureMode: The first failure is to read a woman's anger as a flaw of character and a man's as a response to circumstance, when the same situation may lie behind both. The second is to treat height, a deep voice or a commanding face as evidence of leadership, when they are accidents of the body. The third is to believe the problem lies in how women behave and to advise them to change, when the research places the bias in the people doing the judging. The fourth is to interrupt without noticing, or to let others be cut off without returning to them. The fifth is to praise an idea the second time you hear it without noticing who said it first. And the sixth is to swing to the opposite error, refusing to read anyone's emotion at all, when the aim is to read everyone's by the same standard.

moreCases.title: The registrar who raised her voice
moreCases.scene:
Ngozi, thirty-four, is a surgical registrar in a busy teaching hospital. During an operation on a Tuesday afternoon, she notices that the
  instrument count has been skipped before closing, because the theatre is running late and the consultant wants to finish. She asks for the count.
  Nobody responds. She asks again, louder, and says, "We are not closing until the count is done." The theatre goes quiet. The count is done. It is
  correct.

  Afterwards, the consultant, a senior surgeon in his sixties, tells the theatre manager that Ngozi was "difficult" and "emotional" in front of the
  team, and that she needs to learn how to raise concerns professionally. The comment finds its way into her end-of-placement feedback, where it is
  described as a problem with her communication.

  Hugh, fifty-eight, the clinical director, reads the feedback when Ngozi appeals against it. He knows the consultant well. He also knows that
  the same consultant shouts in theatre most weeks, at juniors, at equipment and at the clock, and that the staff describe him affectionately as
  "old school". Nobody has ever written it in his feedback.

  Hugh asks the theatre manager what happened before Ngozi raised her voice. The theatre manager says that she had asked politely first, and had
  been ignored.

Ngozi has thought about not appealing. A colleague told her that appeals are remembered, and that she should let it go and keep her head down until her next rotation. She appealed anyway, because the comment described a safety check as a character flaw.

Ngozi has heard the consultant described as a brilliant surgeon with a temper, and she agrees with the first half. She has also noticed that when he shouts, the theatre goes quiet and does what he says, and when she raised her voice once, the theatre went quiet and wrote it down.
moreCases.misread:
The consultant read Ngozi's raised voice as a flaw in her character, emotional and difficult, and the comment entered her record as a communication problem. The theatre team had long read his own shouting as a matter of style and the pressure of the job.

The theatre manager, passing on the comment, read it as routine feedback rather than as a judgment that needed checking.

And the person writing her feedback read the consultant's account as the whole story, without asking anyone else in the theatre what they had seen.

Ngozi's colleague, advising her not to appeal, read the system accurately and drew the wrong conclusion from it.
moreCases.betterRead:
Brescoll and Uhlmann found that people put a man's anger down to the situation and a woman's down to her character, and that the gap closed when people were given the situation behind the woman's anger. Here the situation was plain: a skipped safety check, a polite request ignored, and a registrar doing exactly what patient safety requires. Hugh's better reading started with the question the chapter recommends: what happened? He upheld Ngozi's appeal, removed the comment and wrote in her record that she had appropriately insisted on a safety check under time pressure. He also spoke privately to the consultant, and asked him to describe what he would have wanted a junior to do if the count had been wrong.

Hugh also asked the theatre team to agree a simple phrase that anyone, of any grade, could use to pause for a safety check, so that insisting on one would not depend on who raised their voice.

Ngozi completed her placement with a clean record and, two years later, was asked to teach the theatre safety course.

moreCases.title: The trustee who got emotional
moreCases.scene:
Rachel, fifty-two, sits on the board of trustees of a children's charity. At a board meeting, the treasurer proposes moving a large part of
  the charity's reserves into an investment fund that promises higher returns. Rachel, who worked in financial regulation for twenty years, thinks the
  fund is far riskier than it looks, and that losing the reserves would mean closing services. She says so, clearly, and when two other trustees
  brush her objection aside, she says it again with obvious feeling: "I have watched organisations lose everything this way. I am not willing to
  gamble the children's services on it."

  There is a short, uncomfortable silence. The chair, Peter, says, "Let's keep this calm, Rachel," and moves on. The proposal seems set to pass.

  Twenty minutes later, a newer trustee, David, a retired accountant, says that he has been looking at the fund's documents and has some concerns.
  He sets out, calmly and briefly, almost exactly the risks that Rachel described. Several trustees nod. Peter thanks him for a very helpful
  intervention and proposes deferring the decision until the board has independent advice.

  After the meeting, Rachel sits in her car for ten minutes before she drives home. David, who had not noticed what happened, emails her that
  evening to say that he had been building on her point and hoped she did not mind.

Rachel notices, too, that two of the trustees who had brushed her aside are now nodding along with David, and that one of them thanks him for "a calm, clear view".

Peter, for his part, thinks the meeting went well. The board avoided a risky decision, nobody lost their temper, and the new trustee made a useful contribution. He does not remember who first raised the risk.

She has been on boards for fifteen years. She knows that if she mentions it, she risks being told she is being emotional again, and that if she does not, it will happen again next month.
moreCases.misread:
The board read Rachel's feeling as a reason to discount her argument, and Peter read his own "Let's keep this calm" as good chairing. When the same argument arrived calmly from a man, the board read it as a helpful intervention and credited him with it.

Several of the trustees read David's intervention as new information, when it was Rachel's argument in a different voice.

David, too, had read his own point as building on hers, without noticing that the board heard it as new. Good intentions do not change where the credit lands.
moreCases.betterRead:
Salerno and Peter-Hagene found that the same expression of anger from a holdout juror made a man more persuasive and a woman less, even when the words were identical. Rachel's case shows both that pattern and the problem of credit: an idea that passed without weight the first time was praised the second. The better reading would have weighed the argument rather than the feeling, and noticed that the feeling came from expertise. David's email was a start. Peter's better response, when Rachel raised it with him a week later, was to apologise, to say at the next meeting that the deferral had been Rachel's proposal first, and to ask her to lead the review of the board's investment policy. He also began, he said later, asking himself whether he would tell a man to keep calm.

David, when he heard, offered to second Rachel's points at future meetings by name. She said she would rather the chair did his job, but thanked him.

moreCases.title: The manager who was shorter than his team
moreCases.scene:
Danny, thirty-three, has just been promoted to run the night shift at a large distribution warehouse. He is five foot five. One of his team
  leaders, Lee, twenty-six, is six foot three, broad and quiet, and has been on the shift for less than a year. When visiting managers from head office
  walk the floor, they almost always address their questions to Lee. Drivers arriving with problems look for Lee first. Twice, a director has
  congratulated Lee on the shift's improved figures, which were Danny's work.

  Danny has started to compensate. He speaks louder on the floor than he used to, stands on the loading step when he briefs the team, and has
  become sharper in his manner. One of the older workers has begun calling him "the little general" behind his back, and Danny has heard it.

  Lee is uncomfortable too. He has never wanted to be a manager, and he does not know how to tell the director that he is talking to the wrong
  person without sounding as though he is criticising his boss.

  The operations director, Carol, who visits monthly, notices Lee redirecting a driver's question to Danny with a nod of his head. Then she realises,
  with some discomfort, that on her own last visit she had walked straight up to Lee and asked him how the new system was going.

He has also begun to notice that new starters on the shift introduce themselves to Lee first, and that Lee has started to look mortified when they do.

At home, Danny's partner has noticed that he comes back from shifts wound up and tired, and that he has started rehearsing what he will say to the head office managers before they visit, as if preparing for an argument.

When Danny raises it with a friend from another depot, the friend laughs and says he should get some lifts in his boots. Danny laughs too, and feels worse.
moreCases.misread:
The visitors read Lee's height and build as authority and addressed him as the person in charge. When Danny raised his voice and stood on the step, some of the team read his efforts as a small man overcompensating, a reading they would not have made of a tall manager doing the same.

Danny read the nickname as proof that he was failing, and pushed harder, which made it stick.

Carol read her own earlier mistake, once she noticed it, as a small slip. To Danny it had been one more month of being invisible in his own shift.

And the director who congratulated Lee read the figures through the face in front of him, without asking whose they were.
moreCases.betterRead:
Judge and Cable found that taller people earned more, with the link strongest in management and sales, where being seen as a leader matters most. The bias falls on short men as well as on women, and it lives in the people doing the reading. Danny's louder voice was a reasonable response to being overlooked, and it was then read as a flaw, which is a familiar double bind. Carol's better response was to fix her own reading first. On her next visit she went straight to Danny, introduced him to the head office team as the shift manager, and asked him to walk them round. She also asked her managers to begin every site visit by asking who was in charge, rather than assuming. Danny, freed from the competition, let his voice drop. The nickname faded, though not entirely.

Lee was relieved. He told Danny that he had hated being mistaken for the boss and had not known how to stop it.

moreCases.title: The answer that went to the wrong person
moreCases.scene:
Priya, forty-one, is the lead structural engineer on a new bridge for a rail company. She and her graduate engineer, Josh, twenty-five, meet
  the sales engineer from a steel supplier to discuss a problem with the specification of some bolts. Priya has spent a week on the problem and knows
  it in detail. Josh is three months into the job.

  Priya asks the sales engineer a precise technical question about load ratings. He turns, slightly but unmistakably, towards Josh, and answers
  him, looking at him throughout. When Priya asks a follow-up, the man answers Josh again. Josh, embarrassed, keeps glancing at Priya. Priya keeps her
  face still and writes notes. She has had this happen many times before. She has learned that if she points it out, she is seen as touchy, and if she
  does not, the meeting goes on around her.

  On the third question, Josh does something he has not planned. He turns his chair a little towards Priya, so that his body faces her rather than the
  sales engineer, and says, "Priya's the lead on this, she'll know whether that works." Then he looks at her and waits.

  The sales engineer pauses, turns to Priya and answers her for the rest of the meeting.

Josh notices that the sales engineer smiles at him in a friendly, man-to-man way when he answers, as if the two of them were sharing something. It makes him feel slightly sick.

In the car park afterwards, Josh asks Priya whether that happens often. She says it happens in about half of her meetings with new suppliers, and that she has stopped counting because counting made her angry.

Josh also realises that he had felt a small flicker of pleasure at being treated as the expert, before the discomfort set in, and he is not proud of it.
moreCases.misread:
The sales engineer read the younger man as the authority in the room and directed his answers to him, without seeming to notice that he was doing it. Priya read the pattern accurately, but also read that calling it out herself would cost her.

Josh, at first, read his own discomfort as a sign that he should stay out of it.

The sales engineer, if asked, would almost certainly have said that he was simply talking to whoever was easiest to talk to, which is exactly how the bias feels from the inside.
moreCases.betterRead:
When a question is asked in a mixed group, people often address the answer to whoever seems most senior or most confident, and that is frequently a man, regardless of who asked. The correction is small and physical: turn your body and your gaze to the person who asked. Josh did more than that. He used the authority the sales engineer had given him to hand it back, turning towards Priya, naming her role and looking at her, so that the sales engineer's eyes followed his. That is what the chapter means by using whatever advantage you have. Afterwards, Priya thanked him. He said he had felt awkward. She said that was the price of it, and that it was much lower for him than for her.

Josh had not set out to be an ally. He had simply noticed where the man's eyes were going, and moved his own.

workedReading.title: Chairing a promotion panel
workedReading.scene:
Sunil, fifty, is head of engineering at a software company, and this week he chairs the panel that decides promotions to principal engineer. There are three candidates: Elena, thirty-eight, who leads the payments team; Marcus, forty, who leads infrastructure; and Joy, thirty-three, who leads the mobile app. Two other managers sit on the panel with him. Each candidate has a written case, peer feedback and their manager's recommendation. Last year's panel promoted two men and no women from a similar shortlist, and an engineer who left afterwards said in her exit interview that she had been told she was "not quite principal material" without ever being told why. Sunil has read this chapter and wants the panel to judge the evidence rather than the impression each candidate makes in the room.

Sunil also knows his own habits. He tends to warm to candidates who talk the way he does, quickly and with confidence, and he has been told in the past that he gives more airtime to the loudest person on a panel. He has decided to keep a quiet tally of who speaks in the panel itself, as well as judging the candidates.

He also knows that the panel will be tired by the third candidate, and that tired panels fall back on impressions. He schedules a break before each discussion.

steps.label: Agree the criteria first
steps.text:
Before anyone discusses a candidate, Sunil asks the panel to agree what a principal engineer needs to show, with examples: technical judgment, influence across teams, mentoring, delivery. They write them on the whiteboard. He knows that criteria agreed in advance are harder to bend around a first impression, and that an impression formed in the first minute can otherwise become the frame for everything after.

One panellist objects that good engineers can tell a principal when they see one. Sunil agrees that experience matters, and asks him to say what he sees, in words that can go on the board, so that the others can check it against the evidence.

Agreeing the criteria takes twenty minutes, and two of the panel think it is a waste of time. By the end of the day both of them say it was the most useful part.

steps.label: Describe behaviour, not character
steps.text:
When the panel turns to the peer feedback, Sunil asks everyone to underline words that describe character, such as "abrasive", "emotional", "natural leader" or "passionate", and to find the behaviour behind each one. Elena's feedback calls her "abrasive" twice. The behaviour behind it turns out to be that she blocked two releases she judged unsafe. Marcus's feedback calls him "decisive" for doing much the same.

He also asks the panel to treat praise words the same way. "Natural leader" in Marcus's feedback turns out to rest on his running a well-attended weekly meeting, which is worth something, but less than the phrase suggests.

steps.label: Run the swap test
steps.text:
For each loaded word, Sunil asks the panel to imagine the same behaviour from a colleague of a different gender and ask whether they would use the same word. One panellist admits that he would have called Marcus "abrasive" if he had been a woman. They agree to remove character words from their notes and keep the behaviours.

The swap test feels awkward at first, and one panellist says it is political. Sunil says it is about accuracy: if the same behaviour earns different words, at least one of the words is wrong, and they cannot both be evidence.

steps.label: Look for the situation
steps.text:
Joy's feedback includes a comment that she "got upset" in a planning meeting. Sunil asks what happened. Her manager explains that Joy had learned in the meeting that her team's work was being cut without consultation, after six months of effort. The panel agrees that her reaction was a response to a real problem, which she then helped to fix. Brescoll and Uhlmann found that this kind of situational information closes the gap in how anger is judged.

He also asks whether anyone has looked for the situation behind Marcus's "decisive" moments. Two of them turn out to have been decisions that his team later had to reverse.

He reminds the panel that situations are not excuses. They are information about what the behaviour was a response to, which is what the panel needs to judge it.

steps.label: Watch the floor
steps.text:
During the discussion, Sunil keeps an eye on his own panel. He notices that one panellist, Fiona, has tried to speak twice and been talked over both times by the most senior member. He says, "Fiona, you were about to say something about Elena's mentoring," and waits. Fiona points out that Elena has mentored four engineers into senior roles, which nobody else had mentioned.

He also notices that he himself has been looking mostly at the senior panellist when he asks questions, and turns his chair a little so that he can see all three of the others without moving his head.

steps.label: Credit and check
steps.text:
When the senior panellist later makes the same point about mentoring as if it were his own, Sunil says, "That's Fiona's point, and it's a strong one." Before the panel decides, he reads back the evidence for each candidate against each criterion, without the character words, and asks whether anyone's view has changed.

He also reads out the tally he has been keeping of who spoke in the panel. The senior panellist has spoken as much as the other three combined. Nobody says much about it, but the second half of the meeting is noticeably more even.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
The panel promotes Elena and Marcus, and gives Joy a clear plan with two specific gaps to close for next year. Each decision is written up against the criteria, with the evidence. Joy tells Sunil afterwards that it is the first promotion feedback she has had that she could act on. Sunil cannot know whether the panel's decisions were fairer than last year's. He does know that they were made on evidence that everyone could see, and that every loaded word had been examined before it counted.

He shares the panel's method with the other heads of department, with the agreed criteria and the list of loaded words, and suggests that every promotion panel use it next year.

moreFailures.title: Saving your support for afterwards
moreFailures.body:
Many men who notice a colleague being talked over, dismissed or misread do something kind afterwards: a quiet word in the corridor, a message saying "I thought your point was really good." It is well meant, and it is better than nothing. But it leaves the room's reading unchanged. The meeting still ended with her point ignored, her anger recorded as a flaw or her idea credited to someone else, and the people who matter for her career still saw it that way. The private word can even become a substitute for acting, a way of feeling supportive without paying any cost. If you agree with a point, say so in the room, naming the person who made it. If someone is cut off, return to them while the meeting is still running. A short sentence in public does far more than a long one in private.

A useful rule: if you would be happy to say it privately, say it publicly too, in a sentence, at the moment it matters.

If speaking up in the room is genuinely risky for you, say so to the person afterwards, and ask what would help next time.

moreFailures.title: Speaking for her instead of handing back the floor
moreFailures.body:
Some men, wanting to help, restate a woman's point in their own words: "I think what Sara is trying to say is...", and then explain it, often at greater length and with more confidence than she did. The idea may now be heard, but it is heard in his voice, and the room learns that her point needed translating. It can also misstate what she meant. Amplification works differently. It names the person and returns the floor to them: "I want to come back to Sara's point. Sara, can you say more about that?" Then it waits. The aim is not to be the hero of the moment but to make it easier for her to be heard in her own words. If you catch yourself explaining someone else's idea, stop and hand it back.

The same goes for explaining a woman's reaction to the room: "I think Sara's just frustrated" can undermine her as surely as ignoring her.

moreFailures.title: Assuming it is only about gender
moreFailures.body:
This chapter concentrates on gender, because that is where much of the research is. But the same reading errors follow other lines. People read authority into height, a deep voice and a particular accent; they read threat or anger into some faces more readily than others; they interrupt people who are younger, newer, disabled, softly spoken or from a different background. Part V looks at several of these in detail, including how Black men's bodies are read. The swap test works for all of them: imagine the same behaviour from someone different in any of these ways and ask whether your reading would change. If you check only for gender, you may become fairer to some colleagues while still misreading others in exactly the same way.

It also helps to know that people affected by more than one of these patterns at once often face more than the sum of them, which is a good reason to listen to their account of what happens in meetings.

The swap test is quick enough to run several times on the same impression: gender, age, accent, height. Each one may show something.

moreFailures.title: Reading the reaction to bias as the problem
moreFailures.body:
When someone has been interrupted, overlooked or misread repeatedly, they often react: they become curt, they stop contributing, they bring their points in writing, they push harder and louder, or they withdraw from meetings altogether. The reaction is then easy to read as the original problem: she is disengaged, he is aggressive, she is not a team player. That reading turns the effect of the bias into evidence against its target. Danny's louder voice on the warehouse floor and Rachel's ten minutes in her car were both reactions to being misread. Before you judge someone's manner in meetings, look at what happens to them in those meetings. Count the interruptions, notice whose ideas are picked up and ask whether the manner you dislike might be a response to how they have been treated.

Withdrawal is often the cheapest choice left to someone who has been talked over for months. Read it as information about the meeting, not only about the person.

questions.a:
It is a question of accuracy as much as fairness. If you read a colleague's anger as a flaw of character when it was a response to a real problem, you have misread her, and you may also have missed the problem, as Tom did with the untested code and the consultant nearly did with the instrument count. If you promote the tall man because he looks like a leader, you may have passed over the better one. The studies in this chapter do not tell you what to think about anyone. They show that the same behaviour is read differently depending on who shows it, which means that some of your readings are wrong. Correcting them makes you a better judge of people, which is the point of this whole book.

And none of this asks you to stop reading people. It asks you to read everyone by the same standard.

questions.q: What can I do if I am the one who keeps being interrupted?
questions.a:
The research in this chapter places the main responsibility on the people doing the interrupting and on whoever runs the meeting, and it is not your job to fix their habits. Still, some things can help. A calm "I'd like to finish my point" said once, without apology, often works. So does agreeing in advance with a colleague that each of you will return to the other if you are cut off. You can ask the chair to set a norm that people finish before others come in, or to use a round on important items. If the pattern is persistent and affecting your work, it is reasonable to raise it with your manager, using specific examples and counts if you have them, rather than general impressions.

It can also help to keep a short record of incidents, with dates, in case you need it later.

And if you chair meetings yourself, the most powerful change is to make finishing a sentence the norm for everyone.

questions.q: How can I tell whether I am biased if I do not feel biased?
questions.a:
You probably will not feel it, because these biases work in the speed of a first impression, below deliberate thought. That is why the checks in this chapter are deliberate. Read back the words you have used in recent reviews or references, and look for character words such as "emotional", "abrasive", "passionate" or "natural leader", then check whether they cluster by gender. Count interruptions in your own meetings, including your own. Notice where your eyes go when someone asks a question in a group. Run the swap test on your next strong impression. None of this will tell you that you are or are not biased in general. It will show you specific places where your reading may have gone wrong, which is more useful.

Another check is to notice whom you remember as having made a point. If it is usually the loudest or most senior person, look again.

questions.q: Does the backlash research mean women should be assertive only with their bodies?
questions.a:
No. Williams and Tiedens found that explicit dominance, such as direct demands and open disagreement, was penalised in women while nonverbal dominance, such as steady eye contact and a firm voice, was not. It would be easy to turn that into advice for women to say less and stand taller. But that puts the burden in the wrong place. The penalty lies in the people doing the judging, who punish the same behaviour in a woman that they reward in a man. The more useful lesson is for evaluators: when you find yourself disliking a woman's directness, ask whether you would dislike the same directness from a man, and judge the content of what she said.

If you mentor women, it is still reasonable to discuss what tends to land in a particular room. The aim is to share knowledge of the room, not to suggest that she is the problem.

questions.q: How do I amplify someone's point without seeming to speak for them?
questions.a:
Name them, point to their idea and hand the floor back. "I want to come back to what Sara said about the timeline. Sara, can you say more?" Then stop talking and look at her. If an idea is repeated by someone else, credit it simply: "That's close to Sara's point earlier." Avoid restating her idea in your own words at length, which can make it sound as though it needed translating. Avoid making a show of it, too, which can embarrass the person you are trying to help. Done well, amplification is brief, specific and frequent, and after a while it becomes a habit of the group rather than a gesture from one person. It works best when several people do it.

If you are not sure whether someone would welcome amplification, ask them afterwards. Most people will tell you exactly what helps.

Over time, the best sign that amplification is working is that it becomes unnecessary, because the group has learned to hear the first voice.

questions.q: Does height really make that much difference?
questions.a:
It makes a measurable difference on average, though not a decisive one for any individual. Judge and Cable's analysis of four large studies found that taller people earned more, even after accounting for gender, weight and age, and that the link was strongest in sales and management, where being seen as a leader matters most. Each extra inch was worth, on average, several hundred dollars a year. The effect is not about anything a tall person does. It is about how others read height, and it falls on short men as much as on women. If you make decisions about people, the useful question is whether you are responding to what someone has done or to how they look while doing it.

Height is also easy to correct for once you notice it: ask yourself, before a decision, what the person has actually done.

If you are tall, it is worth knowing that some of the deference you receive was not earned, and using it to point attention towards people who did earn it.

watch.title: Hidden Figures: Official Trailer
watch.notice: Three Black women mathematicians at NASA in the 1960s. Watch how their bodies are read in rooms built for others, and how they claim space in them anyway.
